Multi-timeframe analysis

Multi-timeframe analysis means looking at the same chart on more than one timeframe. The higher timeframe gives the context, meaning the main direction and the important zones; the lower timeframe shows in detail how price behaves within that context. A common sequence is to work top down, from 1D to 4H to 1H.

What is multi-timeframe analysis?

A single timeframe shows only one scale of the picture. The 1H chart shows detail but cannot fit a structure lasting weeks on one screen. The 1D chart shows the structure but not how candles behave as price approaches a zone.

In multi-timeframe analysis these scales are read together. The higher timeframe is for context: the trend, important highs and lows, the main zones. The lower timeframe is for detail: how price approaches a zone and how it reacts there.

A common top-down sequence

  1. Set the context on 1D. Note the trend's direction, the last important high and low, and the important zones near price.
  2. Look inside the structure on 4H. See the swings within the daily trend. Check whether the current move is a pullback or a new swing, and where price stands relative to the zones.
  3. Read the detail on 1H. If price is approaching a zone, watch how candles behave there; wicks, closes and small highs and lows show up here.
  4. Write each reading with its timeframe. A summary such as "1D: uptrend. 4H: pullback. 1H: reaction at the support zone" keeps clear which observation belongs to which scale.

Choosing the timeframes

  • Consecutive timeframes are usually 4 to 6 times apart (such as 1D → 4H → 1H). Timeframes too close together show the same thing.
  • Three timeframes are often enough. More can complicate the reading rather than clarify it.
  • Using the same set of timeframes consistently makes readings easier to compare.
  • The higher timeframe gives the context; a single move on a lower timeframe does not replace it.

How timeframes can be read together

They tell the same story

An uptrend on 1D, a pullback to a support zone on 4H, a reaction at that zone on 1H. The three readings fit together.

They point different ways

The rising structure holds on 1D while 1H shows lower highs and lows. This is not an error but two different scales; it is covered on a separate page.

The big picture is sideways

If price moves back and forth in a range on 1D, trends on the lower timeframes often stay within the bounds of that range.

What it shows, what it does not prove

What it shows

  • Where in the larger structure a move is taking place
  • How price behaves in detail at a zone from a higher timeframe
  • Whether readings at different scales fit together

What it does not prove

  • That a move will continue when the timeframes agree
  • That the higher timeframe will always prove right
  • That the chosen set of timeframes is the only correct one

The MarketLevelMap view

How it relates to zones

Zones seen on a higher timeframe cover a longer price history, so they are often treated as more significant. The lower timeframe lets you look inside such a zone: a support zone on the 1D chart shows on the 1H chart as a wide band that many candles move back and forth inside.

That is why reading the zone as a band also makes moving between timeframes easier. The zone is taken from 1D, and where in the band price reacts and closes is followed on 4H and 1H.

Often confused with

  • When timeframes seem to disagreeMulti-timeframe analysis is a way of reading; timeframes pointing in different directions is a common situation you meet while using it.
